name: Azure Logic Apps
oneLiner: Low-code workflow orchestration and integration across 1000+ connectors.
whatItIs: Azure Logic Apps is Azure's low-code workflow and integration service. You build workflows visually in a designer as a trigger plus a series of actions, wiring together Azure services, SaaS apps and on-prem systems through a huge library of pre-built connectors (1000+). It's serverless in the Consumption model — pay per action executed, nothing to run idle. While it overlaps with orchestration, its sweet spot is integration and business-process automation: reacting to events, moving data between systems, and coordinating steps with conditions, loops and error handling. In data platforms it's often used to glue services and trigger pipelines, complementing Data Factory's data-movement focus.

inPractice.narrative: When a file arrives in Blob storage, a Logic App triggers: it calls an API to enrich the data, drops a message on Service Bus that kicks off a Data Factory pipeline, and posts a status to Teams — all built by connecting pre-made connectors in a visual designer, no server to manage. On failure it retries and alerts. Logic Apps is the low-code integrator that reacts to events and coordinates the steps across Azure and SaaS systems.

coreConcepts.detail: Every workflow starts with a trigger (event, schedule, HTTP) followed by actions; you assemble them in a visual designer (or JSON/Bicep) — low-code by design.
Pre-built connectors to Azure services, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, SAP, databases, and on-prem systems (via the on-premises data gateway) make integration the headline strength.
Conditions, switches, loops (for-each), scopes and retry/error-handling policies let workflows branch and recover without code.
Consumption is pay-per-action serverless; Standard runs on the single-tenant Logic Apps runtime (predictable pricing, VNet, local dev) for higher-scale/enterprise needs.
Standard supports stateful workflows (full run history/durability) and stateless (lower latency, less history) — a performance/cost trade-off.
B2B/EDI and message-schema features (Integration Account) support enterprise integration scenarios beyond simple automation.

whenToUse: Low-code integration and automation across Azure, SaaS and on-prem.
Event-driven glue that triggers pipelines and moves data between systems.
Business-process workflows with approvals, notifications and branching.
Connecting to systems where a pre-built connector saves custom code.
Serverless orchestration where a full Airflow/ADF pipeline is unnecessary.
whenNotToUse: Heavy, high-throughput data movement/transformation — use Data Factory.
Complex code-first pipelines with DAGs and backfills — use ADF Managed Airflow.
Purely programmatic orchestration teams prefer to define in code.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Consumption: per action/connector execution; Standard: hosting plan.

pricingShape: Consumption Logic Apps bill per action executed, with premium/enterprise connectors costing more than standard ones — so cost scales with how many actions and which connectors run, and idle workflows cost nothing. Standard runs on a hosting plan (single-tenant Logic Apps runtime) with more predictable, capacity-based pricing plus VNet and local development — better for high-volume or enterprise needs. The levers are choosing Consumption vs Standard by volume, minimising unnecessary actions/connector calls, and watching premium-connector usage, which is a common source of unexpected cost.
gotchas: Premium/enterprise connectors cost more per call — heavy use inflates Consumption bills.
Chatty workflows with many actions add up quickly under per-action pricing.
It's integration-first — for heavy data movement/transform, use Data Factory instead.
On-prem connectivity needs the on-premises data gateway, which you install and maintain.
Consumption vs Standard differ in features (VNet, stateless, pricing) — pick deliberately for scale.
